outcome.candidate_text:
Let \(G\) and \(H\) be arbitrary nonabelian groups of order \(21\).

For \(G\), Sylow’s theorems give
\[
n_7\mid 3,\qquad n_7\equiv1\pmod 7,
\]
so \(n_7=1\). Thus the subgroup \(N=\langle b\rangle\) of order \(7\) is normal. By Cauchy’s theorem, choose \(a\in G\) of order \(3\). Since \(N\cap\langle a\rangle=\{e\}\),
\[
|N\langle a\rangle|=\frac{|N||\langle a\rangle|}{|N\cap\langle a\rangle|}=21.
\]
Hence \(G=N\langle a\rangle\), and every element has a unique expression \(b^s a^r\), where \(0\le s<7\) and \(0\le r<3\).

Because \(N\trianglelefteq G\), conjugation by \(a\) is an automorphism of \(N\), so
\[
aba^{-1}=b^i
\]
for some \(i\in\{1,\dots,6\}\). Since \(a^3=e\), conjugating three times gives \(b=b^{i^3}\), hence \(i^3\equiv1\pmod7\). The solutions are \(i\equiv1,2,4\pmod7\). If \(i=1\), then \(a\) and \(b\) commute; because they generate \(G\), this would make \(G\) abelian. Thus \(i=2\) or \(i=4\). In the latter case, replacing \(a\) by \(a^{-1}\) changes the conjugation exponent to \(4^{-1}\equiv2\pmod7\). Therefore generators \(x,y\) of orders \(3,7\), respectively, can be chosen so that
\[
xyx^{-1}=y^2,
\]
and every element of \(G\) is uniquely \(y^s x^r\).

The same argument applied to \(H\) gives generators \(u,v\) of orders \(3,7\) satisfying
\[
uvu^{-1}=v^2,
\]
with every element of \(H\) uniquely expressible as \(v^s u^r\).

Define
\[
\phi:G\to H,\qquad \phi(y^s x^r)=v^s u^r
\]
for \(0\le s<7\) and \(0\le r<3\). The uniqueness of the normal forms makes \(\phi\) well-defined and bijective. From the defining relation,
\[
x^r y^q x^{-r}=y^{2^r q},
\]
so
\[
(y^s x^r)(y^q x^t)=y^{s+2^r q}x^{r+t},
\]
where exponents are reduced modulo \(7\) and \(3\). The identical formula holds in \(H\), and therefore
\[
\phi\bigl((y^s x^r)(y^q x^t)\bigr)
=v^{s+2^r q}u^{r+t}
=\phi(y^s x^r)\phi(y^q x^t).
\]
Thus \(\phi\) is a bijective homomorphism, so \(G\cong H\). Therefore any two nonabelian groups of order \(21\) are isomorphic.
outcome.stop_reason: Sylow theory provides the unique normal subgroup of order 7, nonabelianness forces the nontrivial conjugation action, and its two possible exponents become identical after inverting the order-3 generator. The resulting unique normal forms give an explicit isomorphism.
